The unit index totals 445,086 units: 79,369 parcel, 282,567 footprint, 83,150 address. The address tier is entirely concentrated in the six non-publishing lower-tier municipalities named in the brief's spec-6.1 note (wainfleet, west lincoln, pelham, grimsby, thorold, port colborne) plus fort erie, lincoln, and niagara-on-the-lake, which likewise publish no parcel or footprint layer we hold - all correctly present, none double-counted against the four municipalities (hamilton, niagara falls, st. catharines, welland) that do have polygon coverage.

Ruling F2 mattered in practice, not just in principle: without it, this run would have silently produced ~171,360 spurious address-tier Hamilton units alongside the 214,293 real footprint ones - a defect of the same shape and comparable scale to the address-anchor defects fixed in §20, and one that would have inflated every later count derived from
(Task 7's aggregation, Task 8's scoring) by construction, not by degree.

Coverage is published as a structured query, not a footnote. Six of twelve Niagara Region lower-tier municipalities publish no parcel or footprint data (wainfleet, west lincoln, pelham, grimsby, thorold, port colborne). Address-tier coverage—via the universal anchor index, supported by every table that carries a civic address—exists across all twelve, plus four neighboring jurisdictions whose addresses appear in the edge rows of the Hamilton and Niagara sources.

The four non-lower-tier labels (county of brant, regional municipality of halton, regional municipality of niagara, wellington county) carry only 11 units total and are noise in the source data—address points mis-tagged with an incorrect
value. They do not block the finding that all twelve lower-tier municipalities are covered at address tier or better.

The unit index is the artefact every later stage consumes: 445,086 parcel, footprint, and address-tier units, each carrying centroid, tier, municipality, area (for parcel/footprint), and provenance. The index is split across 17 municipality labels (13 Niagara Region lower-tier plus 4 noise entries from edge rows in the source), with the finding published that six of twelve Niagara Region municipalities publish no geometry of their own—a data-landscape fact that belongs on the map.

Geocoding against Hamilton's 84-row vacant building registry achieved 86.9% match rate (73/84). The 11 unmatched rows fell into four categories, none representing a defect in the geocoder: (1) highway naming convention drift ("HWY" vs "Highway No."), (2) source data gaps (two rows omit a direction their matching addresses carry), (3) fractional civic numbers (not handled by address normalization), and (4) streets not present in the anchor index at all. A floor of 0.80 is conservative (80% below the 86.9% observed), ensuring the production pipeline never silently ships below this demonstrated capability.

Item 4 is the one worth dwelling on, because the wrong fix was available and looked almost as easy: fold
into their nearest normalized form and move on. That would have been wrong for two different reasons layered on top of each other.
are not Niagara Region or Hamilton at all — they are neighbouring jurisdictions on the Niagara Peninsula (

: the peninsula "extends west to Brantford," i.e. through Brant and Wellington, and Halton borders Hamilton to the north). Relabelling them into a Niagara Region or Hamilton bucket would have manufactured coverage of places the atlas has not verified any data for — the opposite of "a gap is shown as a gap."

is not a stray label at all in the sense the other three are — it is Niagara Region itself, the upper-tier municipality, appearing on an address point where it has no business appearing (an address sits inside a lower-tier municipality, never inside the upper tier that publishes the data).
would strip the "Regional Municipality of" prefix and yield

— a string that reads as if it names a place, but is not one of the twelve lower-tier municipalities and is not Niagara Region either once stripped of its own name. Accepting it into the allow-list under that spelling would have recreated, inside the code, exactly the "Niagara" vs "Niagara Region" collapse that
was written on 2026-08-23 to stop after a finding was published against the wrong jurisdiction. The correct move was to check the

result against the explicit twelve-plus-Hamilton allow-list and exclude anything that fails, whatever spelling produced it — so a future stray label (a thirteenth neighbouring county, a different regional-name variant) is caught by the same rule instead of needing its own patch.

Excluding and counting, rather than dropping silently, matters for the same reason DATA-SOURCES.md's evidence rules exist: "not probed" and "found to be out of scope" are different findings from "does not exist," and only the first two are defensible claims about the world.
